title: Radiators and Weather
premise: Sable Crane, a restaurant critic whose palate died the same year her mother stopped writing to her, has built a career on elegant evasion — reviews that praise everything and commit to nothing. When a box of twenty years of undelivered letters surfaces behind a rented wardrobe, she discovers her mother never stopped writing, and that the letters name a half-brother, Theo, now facing eviction from the family diner by a developer with a court judgment and no conscience. Sable, who has never testified to anything in her life, must finally say what she means — in print, in court, and out loud to a dying woman — before the building, and the last of her family, is demolished.
about_author: Silas Underhill is the pen name of a former line cook who spent a decade writing menus before turning to fiction. He lives above a shuttered diner and writes longhand at the counter.

chapters.title: The Palate
chapters.summary: Sable's POV. She files a glowing, empty review of a restaurant she cannot taste, then learns the landlord is selling the building she's rented for a decade. The beat is quiet dread — the professional mask beginning to crack as the ground literally shifts under her.

chapters.title: Behind the Wardrobe
chapters.summary: Moving out, Sable pries loose a panel and finds a mailbag's worth of letters, all addressed to her, all returned undelivered, spanning twenty years. Her POV. The beat is vertigo — the past arriving all at once, addressed to a person she no longer is.

chapters.title: What Mother Wrote
chapters.summary: Sable reads through the night: her mother's voice, funny and furious, describing a second child — Theo — born after the estrangement, and a diner called Radiators. Sable's POV. The beat is grief braided with betrayal: she was written to, and never written back to.

chapters.title: The Diner at the End of the Block
chapters.summary: Sable travels to her mother's city incognito and eats at Radiators without revealing herself. Theo's POV for the first time — he serves the stranger who has his mother's eyes. The beat is recognition withheld, tenderness under suspicion.

chapters.title: Eviction Notice
chapters.summary: Theo receives the developer's final court date; Sable, still anonymous, watches him absorb it. Alternating POV. The beat is rising injustice — the law working smoothly against the only home Theo has known.

chapters.title: Almost Saying It
chapters.summary: Sable visits her mother in a care home and cannot bring herself to confess who she is; they talk about food, of all things, and her mother says the diner's soup tastes like forgiveness. Sable's POV. The beat is aching near-miss — love that cannot find its sentence.

chapters.title: The Review
chapters.summary: Sable writes, for the first time honestly, a review of Radiators under her own name — and names herself in it. Theo reads it at the counter. Dual POV. The beat is rupture and exposure: identity declared publicly, irrevocably.

chapters.title: Standing
chapters.summary: The developer's lawyer moves to strike Sable's testimony as irrelevant; she argues that a building is a body of evidence — recipes, regulars, a dead father's stove. Courtroom climax. The beat is Sable finally saying it, out loud, at full volume, justice pursued outside and against the law's narrow frame.

chapters.title: Goodbye, Properly
chapters.summary: Her mother, fading, asks the nurse to bring in 'the girl from the review.' Sable reads the letters aloud to her, answers twenty years of them in one sitting, and says goodbye properly. Sable's POV. The beat is catharsis — taste returning, faintly, with salt.

chapters.title: Radiators and Weather
chapters.summary: Weeks later: the diner stands, the judgment overturned on procedural grounds Sable's testimony forced into daylight. Sable and Theo cook together, awkwardly, in the kitchen. Her POV. The beat is resolution — a found family at a counter, weather changing, soup on the stove.
